body: There is a construct substitution at the heart of this spec, and it should be named plainly. The research question asks whether 'working memory LOAD' moderates the discounting-procrastination relationship. Load is an experimental manipulation — the number of items held in memory, 1-back versus 3-back. What the spec actually measures is working memory CAPACITY, a stable individual-difference variable extracted from n-back accuracy and reaction time. These are not the same thing, and the spec quietly concedes this in its assumptions ('there is no random assignment to load conditions in the aggregated dataset'). The moderation analysis as specified (FR-004) therefore answers a different question than the one validated in the project idea: it tests whether people with better WM show a weaker discounting-procrastination association, not whether cognitive load exacerbates it. The validation checks above were run against the original question; the spec operationalizes a revised one, and no check flags the substitution. Second, a quantitative defect: the sensitivity sweep in FR-007 varies the cutoff by ±0.05*SD and ±0.10*SD around the median. A shift of 0.05 standard deviations moves the split point by roughly 2% of the distribution — these are effectively identical subgroup definitions, so the 'sensitivity analysis' will nearly always confirm stability regardless of whether the finding is real. A meaningful sweep would span at least ±0.5*SD, or better, report the interaction as continuous and drop the arbitrary binary split entirely, since FR-004 already models WM as continuous — the binary subgroup analysis is redundant machinery. Third, SC-004 is internally muddled: it says sensitivity is 'measured against the variation in the interaction p-value' but then declares instability by whether 'the confidence interval for the interaction effect crosses zero' — a p-value criterion and a CI criterion stated as one, with no rule for reconciling them.
